title: Sources of EU Law and Hierarchy

slides.title: Primary and secondary — and more
slides.text: The two familiar boxes, with the lecturer's teaser: there is more than primary and secondary law. What is missing is tertiary law and soft law, both of which come later in this lecture.

slides.title: What primary law consists of
slides.text: Four components: the TEU and TFEU themselves; the protocols annexed to them, which have the same legal value; the Charter of Fundamental Rights; and the general principles of law.

cards.q: What belongs to EU primary law?
cards.a: The TEU and TFEU, the protocols annexed to them (same legal value as the Treaties), the Charter of Fundamental Rights, and the general principles of EU law.

slides.title: What is in the TEU and what is in the TFEU
slides.text: A division worth knowing, because an exam question naming a topic expects the right Treaty. The TEU carries the constitutional frame: the objective of ever closer union, the Union's values, its tasks, the basic tasks of institutions and member states, fundamental rights, the institutions and their basic structure, the CFSP, the Union's legal personality, treaty amendment, accession and withdrawal, and the scope of application. The TFEU carries the machinery: the catalogue of competences and cross-cutting principles, the internal policies in detail — citizenship, internal market, competition, external trade — and the detailed rules on the institutions, including the legislative and court procedures.

cards.q: Which Treaty contains the catalogue of competences and which contains the values of the Union?
cards.a: The catalogue of competences and the detailed policies are in the TFEU; the Union's values, objectives, basic institutional structure, accession and withdrawal are in the TEU.

slides.title: How primary law is changed
slides.text: Three routes under Article 48 TEU. The ORDINARY revision procedure (Art 48(1)-(5)) in two variants — with a Convention, or without one under Article 48(3) second subparagraph. The SIMPLIFIED procedures (Art 48(6) and (7)): revision of the internal policies in Part III TFEU, and the two general passerelle clauses. And separately, accession and withdrawal under Articles 49 and 50 TEU. The common feature of the ordinary route is that any change needs ratification by all member states.

cards.q: Name the routes for amending EU primary law.
cards.a: The ordinary revision procedure under Art 48(1)-(5) TEU, with or without a Convention; the simplified procedures under Art 48(6) for Part III TFEU and Art 48(7) passerelles; plus accession and withdrawal under Arts 49 and 50 TEU.

slides.title: Article 49 TEU: who may join
slides.text: Only a EUROPEAN state may accede — and the Treaties deliberately do not define where European states are located, which is why Morocco's 1987 application was rejected and why Turkey's candidacy is legally possible. Accession is only possible to the Union as a whole; there is no partial membership. Two sets of conditions: the applicant must respect and promote the values of Article 2 TEU, and must meet the Copenhagen criteria, to which Article 49(1) fourth subparagraph refers.

cards.q: What are the two conditions for accession under Article 49 TEU?
cards.a: The applicant must be a European state that respects and promotes the values of Article 2 TEU, and it must meet the conditions of eligibility agreed by the European Council — the Copenhagen criteria. Accession is only to the Union as a whole.

slides.title: The Copenhagen criteria
slides.text: From the Council's Copenhagen conclusions of 22 June 1993. POLITICAL: stability of institutions guaranteeing democracy, the rule of law, human rights and respect for and protection of minorities. ECONOMIC: a functioning market economy able to cope with competitive pressure and market forces within the Union. ACQUIS: ability to take on the obligations of membership, including the aims of political, economic and monetary union. And ABSORPTION CAPACITY: the Union's own capacity to absorb new members while maintaining the momentum of integration — a criterion about the Union, not the candidate.

terms.def: Political, economic, acquis and absorption-capacity conditions for EU accession, agreed in June 1993.

cards.q: Name the four Copenhagen criteria and say which one is not about the candidate.
cards.a: Political (democracy, rule of law, human rights, minority protection), economic (functioning market economy able to withstand competitive pressure), acquis (capacity to take on membership obligations), and absorption capacity — the last concerns the Union's own ability to take in new members.

slides.title: Accession phase 1: becoming a candidate
slides.text: The diagram: a third country submits an APPLICATION to the Council; the Council notifies the European Parliament and the national parliaments and consults the European Commission; the Parliament must give its CONSENT; and the Council decides. Only then is the state a candidate country.

slides.title: Phase 1, completed
slides.text: The same diagram with the applicant now labelled 'candidate country'.

slides.title: Accession phase 2: negotiations
slides.text: The Commission proposes a negotiating framework; the Council adopts the negotiating mandate; and negotiations with the candidate proceed chapter by chapter through SCREENING of the acquis, divided into 35 chapters, with the Commission reporting back to the Council. The chapters are opened and closed individually, which is what allows a single member state to block progress.

terms.def: Chapter-by-chapter examination of the candidate's law against the 35 chapters of the EU acquis.

cards.q: Into how many chapters is the acquis divided in accession negotiations, and why does that matter politically?
cards.a: 35 chapters, opened and closed one at a time. Because each step needs member state agreement, a single member state can block the process chapter by chapter.

slides.title: The accession process step by step
slides.text: A reference to the Commission's own enlargement pages.

slides.title: Accession phase 3: the Accession Treaty
slides.text: Article 49(2) TEU: an agreement between the member states and the applicant. It has two parts. The ACCESSION TREATY fixes accession at a specific date. The ACT OF ACCESSION contains the adaptations to primary and secondary Union law that accession requires — integrating the new member state into the Union, with safeguard clauses and transitional provisions — together with the conditions of admission.

slides.title: Accession phase 4: ratification
slides.text: The treaty must be ratified by all existing member states and by the new one. And the small factual detail the lecturer likes to ask: the instruments of ratification are deposited with the GOVERNMENT OF THE ITALIAN REPUBLIC, under Article 54(1) TEU — because the founding Treaty of Rome was signed there.

cards.q: With whom are the instruments of ratification of EU treaties deposited?
cards.a: With the Government of the Italian Republic (Art 54(1) TEU) — a legacy of the Treaty of Rome.

slides.title: Withdrawal: Article 50 TEU
slides.text: The slide shows the Brexit timeline from the Council's own site. The structure of Article 50: a member state may decide to withdraw in accordance with its own constitutional requirements; it notifies the European Council; the Union negotiates a withdrawal agreement, concluded by the Council by qualified majority with Parliament's consent; and the Treaties cease to apply from the date of entry into force of the agreement or, FAILING THAT, two years after notification unless the European Council unanimously agrees to extend. That automatic two-year cliff is the provision's most important feature — it puts the pressure of time on the withdrawing state.

terms.def: The withdrawal clause: notification, negotiated withdrawal agreement, and automatic expiry of the Treaties two years after notification unless extended unanimously.

cards.q: What happens under Article 50 TEU if no withdrawal agreement is concluded?
cards.a: The Treaties cease to apply to the withdrawing state two years after its notification, unless the European Council, in agreement with that state, unanimously decides to extend the period.

slides.title: General principles of EU law
slides.text: Where they come from: the TELOS of the Treaties — their purpose and system — and the common legal tradition of the member states, with the Court of Justice confirming and shaping them through case law. The question mark on the slide over 'confirmed by CJEU case law' points at the standing criticism: the Court both finds and makes these principles.

cards.q: From what two sources does the Court derive the general principles of EU law?
cards.a: The telos and system of the Treaties, and the common legal traditions of the member states — with the Court's own case law confirming and developing them.

slides.title: Secondary law: the five acts of Article 288 TFEU
slides.text: Regulation, directive, decision — binding. Recommendation, opinion — not binding. The next three slides give the definitions, which should be known verbatim.

slides.title: Regulations
slides.text: Article 288(2) TFEU: a regulation shall have GENERAL APPLICATION, shall be BINDING IN ITS ENTIRETY and DIRECTLY APPLICABLE in all member states. Three properties, and all three matter. General application distinguishes it from a decision; binding in its entirety distinguishes it from a directive; direct applicability means it becomes law in the member states without — indeed generally forbidding — any national transposition.

terms.def: A regulation becomes part of national law automatically on entry into force, without and generally excluding national transposition.

cards.q: Give the definition of a regulation in the words of Article 288(2) TFEU.
cards.a: A regulation has general application, is binding in its entirety, and is directly applicable in all member states.

cards.q: A member state re-enacts a regulation word for word in national law. Is that permissible?
cards.a: As a rule no. A regulation is directly applicable; reproducing it nationally obscures its EU origin and endangers uniform application, and the Court has held such transposition impermissible.

slides.title: Directives
slides.text: Article 288(3) TFEU: a directive shall be binding, AS TO THE RESULT TO BE ACHIEVED, upon each member state to which it is addressed, but shall leave to the national authorities the choice of FORM AND METHODS. Hence transposition into national law — and hence the whole problem of what happens when a member state fails to transpose in time, which is where direct effect, indirect effect and state liability come from.

terms.def: The national legislation by which a member state gives effect to a directive within the implementation deadline.

cards.q: Give the definition of a directive under Article 288(3) TFEU and say what follows from it.
cards.a: A directive is binding as to the result to be achieved upon each member state addressed, but leaves the choice of form and methods to national authorities. It therefore requires transposition — and failure to transpose generates the doctrines of direct effect, indirect effect and state liability.

slides.title: Decisions
slides.text: Article 288(4) TFEU: a decision shall be binding in its entirety; a decision which specifies those to whom it is addressed shall be binding only on them. So a decision may be addressed — to a member state or a company, as in competition cases — or unaddressed, in which case it binds generally. It is the instrument for individual cases.

cards.q: How does a decision differ from a regulation?
cards.a: Both are binding in their entirety, but a regulation has general application, while a decision that names its addressees binds only them. A decision is the instrument for individual cases.

slides.title: Tertiary law
slides.text: Two instruments below secondary law: delegated acts under Article 290 TFEU and implementing acts under Article 291 TFEU.

slides.title: Delegated acts (Art 290 TFEU)
slides.text: Non-legislative acts of general application adopted by the Commission to update or SUPPLEMENT non-essential parts of a legislative act, under the oversight of Parliament and Council. Three limits: they cannot change the ESSENTIAL elements of the legislative act; the legislative act must define the objectives, content, scope and duration of the delegation; and Parliament and Council may revoke the delegation or object to the delegated act. That last control is what distinguishes them from implementing acts.

cards.q: What are the three limits on delegated acts under Article 290 TFEU?
cards.a: They may not alter the essential elements of the legislative act; the legislative act must define the objectives, content, scope and duration of the delegation; and Parliament and Council may revoke the delegation or object to the act.

slides.title: Adoption of delegated acts
slides.text: An infographic from the Council showing the objection and revocation stages.

slides.title: Implementing acts (Art 291 TFEU)
slides.text: Start from the default: primary responsibility for implementing EU law lies with the MEMBER STATES. Only where UNIFORM conditions for implementation are needed — taxation, agriculture, the internal market, health and food safety — does the Commission, or exceptionally the Council under Articles 24 and 25 TEU, adopt an implementing act. The control here is not by Parliament and Council but by committees of member state representatives, which is why the process is called comitology.

terms.def: Control of the Commission's implementing acts by committees of member state representatives.

cards.q: Who implements EU law as a rule, and when does the Commission adopt an implementing act instead?
cards.a: The member states implement as a rule. The Commission adopts an implementing act only where uniform conditions for implementation are needed (Art 291 TFEU) — exceptionally the Council under Arts 24-25 TEU.

cards.q: What is the control mechanism for delegated acts, and what for implementing acts?
cards.a: Delegated acts: Parliament and Council may object or revoke the delegation. Implementing acts: committees of member state representatives — comitology.

slides.title: Soft law
slides.text: Instruments the institutions use to pursue policy objectives which are not legally binding but have practical and indirect legal effects: they shape behaviour and influence how binding measures are applied, and they can have SELF-BINDING effects on the institution that issued them — a Commission that announces guidelines cannot simply ignore them without reasons. Examples: recommendations, opinions, green and white papers, action plans, communications, guidelines and notices.

cards.q: In what sense can EU soft law bind, despite not being binding?
cards.a: Indirectly — it shapes behaviour and the application of binding rules — and through self-binding: an institution that publishes guidelines limits its own discretion and cannot depart from them arbitrarily.

slides.title: Two hierarchy questions
slides.text: Hierarchy means two different things and the exam distinguishes them: the relationship WITHIN EU law, between its own sources; and the relationship BETWEEN EU law and member state law, which is the topic of primacy.

slides.title: The hierarchy, drawn
slides.text: From the top: primary law; then international agreements concluded by the Union; then secondary law; then tertiary law; and below all of it, member state law. The bracket on the side — 'integration proof core' of the member states, with a question mark — marks the contested claim of national constitutional courts that some core of national constitutional identity stands outside this order. Note the position of international agreements: below primary law, but above secondary law, which means an EU act can be annulled for conflicting with an agreement the Union concluded.

terms.def: The claim of national constitutional courts that a core of constitutional identity is beyond the reach of EU law; contested by the CJEU.

cards.q: Where do international agreements concluded by the Union sit in the hierarchy of EU law?
cards.a: Below primary law but above secondary law — so a regulation or directive can be challenged for incompatibility with an agreement the Union has concluded.

slides.title: Conflicts within primary law
slides.text: Within primary law there is no internal hierarchy, so the general rules apply: lex specialis and lex posterior — the same two maxims met in the international law half of the course.

cards.q: Two provisions of primary EU law conflict. How is the conflict resolved?
cards.a: By the general rules, since primary law has no internal hierarchy: lex specialis derogat legi generali and lex posterior derogat legi priori.

slides.title: Conflicts within secondary law
slides.text: The same answer one level down: within secondary law, lex specialis and lex posterior decide. A directive does not outrank a regulation, nor the reverse — the form of the act says nothing about its rank.

cards.q: Does a regulation rank above a directive?
cards.a: No. Both are secondary law of the same rank; conflicts between them are resolved by lex specialis and lex posterior, not by the type of instrument.

slides.title: ANY member state law
slides.text: The diagram emphasises the word ANY: every level of EU law stands above every level of member state law, including national constitutions. That is the claim primacy makes, and the next lecture is devoted to it.

slides.title: Three limits in one picture
slides.text: The closing slide sets three concepts beside each other, and they are the three ways an EU act can be attacked or resisted. COMPETENCE — did the Union have the power at all? PRIMACY, and its shadow ULTRA VIRES — does EU law prevail, and what if a national court says the Union acted beyond its powers? And the INTEGRATION-PROOF CORE — is there national constitutional ground EU law cannot reach? The first is settled law; the second and third are the live constitutional conflict between the Court of Justice and national constitutional courts.

terms.def: A national constitutional court's claim to review whether an EU act exceeded the competences conferred.

cards.q: What are the three lines of attack against the application of an EU act in a member state?
cards.a: Lack of competence (the Union never had the power); ultra vires review by a national constitutional court (the Union exceeded the powers conferred); and the claimed integration-proof core of national constitutional identity.
